title: TB8-16509
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I allow this appeal.

XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of South Africa. He claims that he fears returning to South Africa due to his sexual orientation, his race, and his membership in a particular social group as a white XXXX. He also fears persecution from three individuals that he reported for criminal activity.
The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the Appellant had established his claims regarding his sexual orientation, but that he has an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Cape Town.

The Appellant alleges that the IFA should be reassessed due to new circumstances in South Africa and due to errors in the RPD's assessment. The Appellant has submitted new evidence to support his appeal and he is requesting an oral hearing.
I find that the Appellant's sexual orientation, and not the other aspects of his profile, put him at risk in South Africa. I further find that he does not have a safe IFA.
The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellant is a Convention1 refugee. NEW EVIDENCE The evidence presented by the Appellant is accepted

According to the law,2 I can only accept evidence that: i. arose after the RPD decision; or ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.3

The Appellant has submitted the following articles: - from The Citizen, "Khoi-San king declares that the Cape has seceded from SA", dated July 17, 2018. - from South Africa Today, "The Cape is now The Sovereign State of Good Hope", dated July 16, 2018.

Both articles are regarding an event that occurred after the RPD's decision. The Appellant argues that this event is related to an assessment of the proposed IFA. For these reasons, I will accept the articles into evidence. A Hearing is Not Warranted
As the newly submitted and accepted evidence does not raise questions regarding the Appellant's credibility, I will not hold a hearing.4 ANALYSIS
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.5
When assessing this case, I took into consideration the Chairperson's Guideline 9: Proceedings Before the IRB Involving Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression6 (SOGIE Guideline).

The RPD found that the Appellant was credible, and that had established his sexual orientation. I have reviewed these findings and found no errors; I therefore adopt these findings as my own. The determinative issue is whether there is a viable IFA. I find that the Appellant does not have a viable IFA in South Africa, my reasons for these findings are below. The new evidence does not indicate a requirement to reassess the IFA
The Appellant's new evidence does not speak to the current conditions in South Africa. Therefore, the new evidence does not indicate a reason to reassess Cape Town as an IFA.

The Appellant argues that the new evidence regarding the secession of Cape province potentially negates the RPD's finding that the Appellant can relocate to Cape Town as an IFA. The articles indicate that there was a declaration of secession of the Cape province, of which Cape Town is a part, made by the king of the Khoi-San kingship. As part of this declaration, an eviction notice was served on the Parliament in the province. The Appellant acknowledged in his appeal memorandum that this was a developing story, and the long-term legal implications of this secession process were unclear. The Appellant argues that the fact that a secession process was initiated warrants a revisiting of the IFA issue, as the premise of an IFA finding is that a person has a legal right to relocate within the country. However, if this secession process were to be ratified, this premise would likely no longer hold.

By the Appellant's own assertions, this was a potential, not actual, secession. The current country documents make no mention of this secession. This argument was speculative at the time of the Appellant's memorandum, and now there is no evidence that the secession, in fact, occurred. For these reasons, I find that a past, potential secession of Cape province is not relevant to the discussion of the Appellant's forward-facing risk in Cape Town. The RPD did not rely on relativity to assess the IFA

The RPD did not indicate that Cape Town is a safe IFA simply because it was safer than the rest of South Africa. The RPD assessed whether South Africa was safe for the Appellant, who has a diverse SOGIE, and then assessed whether Cape Town is a safe IFA.

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by relying on the fact that Cape Town is relatively safer than other areas in the South Africa. The Appellant argues that, to establish that a viable IFA exists, a decision maker must be able to demonstrate that the situation in the IFA is qualitatively different than the situation in other parts of the country where there exists a reasonable chance of persecution.

When assessing whether Cape Town is a safe IFA, the RPD considered both the safety of individuals with a diverse SOGIE in South Africa as a whole, and in Cape Town in particular. The RPD found that South Africa has some of the most progressive legislation in the world to protect individuals with a diverse SOGIE and that the government is seeking to bolster anti-discrimination laws. The RPD found that in general, LGBTQ persons in South Africa are not subject to treatment by the state which would be persecutory or cause serious harm, and that while LGBTQ people may face some form of discrimination, harassment and violence from societal actors, the evidence does not establish that they are generally at risk of serious harm or persecution from non-state actors.

Within that context, the RPD found that, while the situation for LGBTQ people in South Africa is not perfect, and that there is discrimination and harassment, the Appellant would be able to live safely in Cape Town, on a balance of probabilities, which is a more tolerant and welcoming place for the LGBTQ community and is in fact a destination for people in the LGBTQ community.

The Appellant's characterization that the RPD's assessment that Cape Town was merely better than the rest of the country, but was still not safe, is not a correct summation of the RPD's findings. The RPD first assessed the safety of individuals with a diverse SOGIE in South Africa in general, and then found that Cape Town is a particular good candidate for a safe IFA. For these reasons, I do not find that RPD used relativity to assess the IFA. Profile assessment

The RPD did not err by not assessing the combined effects of the Appellant's profile as a white XXXX, and member of the LGBTQ community. However, I find that the Appellant's profile as a rape survivor should be assessed along with his sexual orientation when assessing the safety of any IFA.

The Appellant argues that the RPD also erred globally in its assessment of the forward-facing risk faced by the Appellant in that it artificially separated the aspects of the Appellant's profile rather than considering it holistically as giving rise to a specific risk profile.

The Appellant is correct that a claimant's entire profile should be considered to ensure that any combined effects which could affect the claimant's risk in a potential IFA are assessed. However, each of the different elements of a claimant's profile must be established for the combined effects to be assessed. In this case, the RPD found that the Appellant had established his sexuality but found that he had not established that he faced a risk due to his race, and he had not established that his employment or livelihood as a XXXX is not central to his identity. For these reasons, I find that the RPD did not err by not assessing the combined effects of elements of the Appellant's profile that were not established.

However, I find that the RPD erred by not assessing the Appellant's profile as a rape survivor, along with his diverse SOGIE, and I will do that assessment below. The Appellant does not have a viable IFA in South Africa
The Appellant's sexual orientation puts him at risk in South Africa, and state protection against sexual assault is not available for individuals with a diverse SOGIE.

The Appellant argues that the objective evidence shows that the rights given to LGBTQ South Africans on paper are illusory and theoretical. The Appellant submits that the RPD misapprehended his evidence with respect to whether he was able to live openly as a gay man in South Africa. The Appellant argues it is trite law that state protection cannot be based on state efforts or intentions alone.
The Appellant has established that he is a gay man and a rape survivor.7 He described being laughed at by police when he went to them to report the incident.8

The country documents indicate that: - Despite the robust laws and policies protecting LGBT persons' rights some government officials, including police, health workers and educators, reportedly discriminate against persons because of their actual or perceived gender identity and/or sexual orientation. Some members of the police service have also been reported to have ridiculed, harassed, physically attacked and raped LGBT persons, particularly lesbians. Homophobic attitudes also negatively affect how the police handle complaints by LGBT persons.9 - The enforcement of the law is the responsibility of the South Africa Police Service (SAPS). While the SAPS continues to professionalize it is reported to be understaffed, ill equipped, poorly trained, and affected by corruption. Some members of the police force have reportedly discriminated against, harassed, physically attacked and raped LGBT persons.10 - The US State Department report on human rights in 2016 observed that: 'There were reports of official mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity despite clear government policies prohibiting discrimination. Security force members, for example, reportedly raped LGBTI persons during arrest.11 - The Freedom House's Freedom in the World report covering events in 2016 observed: 'South Africa has one of the world's most liberal legal environments for LGBT (lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender) people... However, there are frequent reports of physical attacks against LGBT people, including instances of so-called corrective rape, in which lesbians are raped by men who claim that the action can change the victim's sexual orientation.12 - Although instances of corrective rape of men are thought to be uncommon, a 2003 study conducted by Out LGBT Well-Being (Out) and the University of South Africa Centre for Applied Psychology (UCAP) observed: 'We found that the percentage of black gay men who said they have experienced corrective rape matched that of the black lesbians who partook in the study,' says Professor Juan Nel, a specialist in hate-crime criminology at UCAP.13

On a balance of probabilities, I find that the country documents as excerpted above indicate that, while South Africa is certainly working towards greater protections for individuals with a diverse SOGIE, there is still a serious possibility for harm, and there is a strong indication that state protection is not available. I found no evidence that the Appellant's profile as a rape survivor puts him at a greater risk for rape in the future, however I did find that the country documents support his allegation that the police treated him poorly and did not investigate when he was raped.

For these reasons, I find that there is a seriously possibility that the Appellant could be harmed in South Africa due to his sexual orientation, and that he therefore has a well-founded fear of persecution. Further arguments

The Appellant has also made arguments regarding the RPD's findings that he was not at risk in South Africa due to his race and occupation. As I have found that the Appellant is a refugee due to his sexual orientation, I will not thoroughly detail my findings regarding these arguments. I note here, however, that I have reviewed the RPD's findings regarding these aspects of the Appellant's claim and I found no errors.

The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellant is a Convention refugee.
